st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source analyses information design in credence-good markets, not legal AI capability, verification, human–AI work allocation or operating-model redesign. Its findings about limited signals, comprehension and diagnostic noise may be analogically relevant, but they do not establish a position on the cluster’s proposition.

st.t: Credence incentives: More information may not improve service
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s incentive-and-information framing and materially extends it with a continuous-loss model. It shows that even precise consumer inference can coexist with inefficient outcomes, while a deliberately designed binary signal can achieve the first best when experts can choose an information structure. This supports the claim that more information alone need not improve expert services, while identifying information design as a conditional remedy rather than asserting that less information is generally better.

st.t: Expert matching: Observable work may remain unsuitable
st.an: The paper accepts the cluster’s framing of expert services as credence goods where observable work may not reveal whether service was necessary. It materially extends the synthesis by modelling diagnostic information as an endogenous design choice: inefficient equilibria persist even with precise inference, but a deliberately coarse binary diagnostic signal can conditionally restore first-best efficiency. This is a theoretical contribution rather than empirical evidence and rests on restrictive assumptions.

It also materially sharpens the distinction between verifying promised work and imposing liability for resolving the underlying problem, showing why observability alone need not ensure suitable treatment.

kp.k: Credence goods create persistent client information disadvantages
kp.d: The authors identify legal service alongside repair, financial advice and healthcare as credence goods: consumers cannot ascertain service necessity or value even after purchase. The article develops a general economic framework rather than studying AI or documenting changes in legal practice.
qs: Credence goods and services have qualities and values unobserved by consumers before and after purchase or consumption.
Consumers face the same challenge when they need appliance repair, ﬁnancial advice, healthcare consultation, and legal service.

kp.k: Continuous losses and endogenous diagnosis extend binary models
kp.d: The model replaces the conventional two-problem, two-treatment setup with continuously distributed losses and allows experts to choose diagnostic precision. Its findings are theoretical, not empirical; the continuous setup is intended to represent complex problems and permit richer strategic behaviour.
qs: First, we expand the binary model to allow for a continuum of losses.
Second, we endogenize the expert’s diagnosis precision.
No data was used for the research described in the article.

kp.k: Outcome liability and unverifiable costs define the model
kp.d: A risk-neutral expert privately observes the loss and offers a repair price to a risk-neutral consumer. Acceptance obliges the expert to eliminate the loss, but neither loss nor repair cost is observable to the consumer. Initially, cost increases deterministically with loss, and repair is efficient only below a threshold. These assumptions delimit the results rather than describing all expert services.
qs: We assume that the expert is liable for the repair, and that treatment cost is not veriﬁable, so our work belongs to the ﬁrst line of the literature.
The only veriﬁable event is that a repair avoids the loss, so the expert must perform the repair once the price oﬀer is accepted.

kp.k: Perfect private diagnosis produces inefficient equilibria
kp.d: Under the baseline model, all perfect-Bayesian equilibria leave some efficiently repairable losses untreated. Incentive compatibility requires acceptance probabilities and expert profits to weakly decrease with loss, while transaction prices weakly increase. Fully efficient treatment cannot be sustained when the expert privately knows the exact loss.
qs: Propositions 1 to 2 together show that all equilibria are ineﬃcient.
Parts i) and ii) together say that as the loss and cost increase, the price increases but the acceptance rate decreases.
Part iii) further says that the equilibrium proﬁt must decrease with losses; again, this follows from proﬁts varying inversely with costs.

kp.k: Pooling prices leave higher efficient repairs undone
kp.d: The principal pooling equilibrium uses one price for losses below an endogenous cutoff and refuses repair above it. The price equals both conditional average loss and repair cost at the cutoff; consumers accept it with certainty. Because consumers value the pool at its average while the expert considers marginal repair cost, the cutoff falls below the efficient threshold—a mechanism the authors compare to Akerlof’s lemons problem.
qs: The recommended price is the consumer’s average valuation conditional on losses being below the threshold, and this price is also the expert’s repair cost at the threshold.
Because of the discrepancy between marginal and average, the pooling equilibrium will leave some high losses unrepaired ineﬃciently.

kp.k: Belief refinement selects the maximal pooling equilibrium
kp.d: Other pooling equilibria can be supported by optimistic off-path beliefs. The authors introduce the Nonnegative Profit Principle: after an off-equilibrium offer, consumers use the prior restricted to losses whose repair costs do not exceed that price. This refinement eliminates lower-cutoff pooling equilibria but does not eliminate every hybrid equilibrium.
qs: According to the Nonnegative Proﬁt Principle, the consumer believes that the expert’s price at least covers cost.
Then, we introduce the Nonnegative Proﬁt Principle belief reﬁnement to reject all these other pooling equilibria except the one in Proposition 2.
We show that the Nonnegative Proﬁt Principle reﬁnement can eliminate some, but not all, hybrid equilibria.

kp.k: Truthful price signals require probabilistic consumer rejection
kp.d: In the unique separating equilibrium, prices equal losses and thereby reveal them. Consumers must reject higher prices with increasingly high probabilities to discourage experts from charging high-loss prices for low-loss problems. This produces undertreatment except at the lowest loss. The authors regard the finely calibrated randomisation as demanding and potentially unrealistic.
qs: We also derive a unique separating equilibrium, in which the expert charges the consumer her loss from the problem, so the consumer can infer losses from prices.
The consumer rejects each price with a positive probability that increases in the oﬀered price.
The equilibrium does require the consumer to ﬁne tune the acceptance probability according to the solution of a diﬀerential equation.

kp.k: Coarse disclosure can outperform full disclosure
kp.d: Neither pooling nor separation universally dominates: the ranking depends on the loss distribution and cost function. Pooling repairs low losses more reliably; separation sometimes repairs higher losses that pooling excludes. Since expected consumer surplus is zero in the two principal equilibria, expert-profit and social-surplus rankings coincide. This contrasts with the binary-model result attributed to Fong (2005), where truthful separation maximises expert profit.
qs: Because consumer surplus is zero in both equilibria, comparing proﬁts across the two equilibria is the same as comparing social surpluses.
Depending on the loss distribution and cost functions, pooling equilibrium proﬁt may be higher or lower than separating equilibrium proﬁt.
Fong (2005) shows that the expert’s proﬁt and eﬃciency is maximized by the separating equilibrium.

kp.k: Coarse diagnostic acquisition can restore first-best efficiency
kp.d: When the expert publicly chooses a diagnostic information structure before privately receiving its signal, a binary signal identifying whether repair is efficient implements the first best. The expert quotes conditional average loss for the efficient group and refuses the other group. This commits pricing to average costs rather than privately observed marginal costs, preventing cream skimming. The expert captures all expected surplus, so efficiency does not imply increased expected consumer surplus.
qs: The expert will optimally choose imperfect diagnostic information even when information acquisition is costless.
The expert can implement the ﬁrst best and extract the entire surplus from trade by the information structure in (5) or (6).
Using a binary signal, the expert commits to using average-cost information to make price oﬀers, and achieves the ﬁrst best.

kp.k: Efficient coarse diagnosis requires demanding information conditions
kp.d: The first-best result requires the diagnostic test to be common knowledge and the expert to learn the actual loss during repair, after agreeing the price and remaining liable for completion. Some repairs then lose money ex post. The authors caution that consumers may not understand tests or signals. Their noisy-test extension permits both excessive and insufficient repair, converging to first best as noise disappears.
qs: Proposition 5 is not meant to report an optimism that the simple diagnostic test entirely solves credence-good problems.
The analytical result notwithstanding, the extensive form does require the expert’s choice of a diagnostic test be common knowledge.
With imperfect tests, both excessive and insuﬃcient repair can occur in equilibrium.
As the noise vanishes, the equilibrium outcome converges to the ﬁrst best.

kp.k: Random-cost pricing reflects costs rather than observed losses
kp.d: In the extension where experts privately observe both random repair costs and consumer losses, any positively accepted equilibrium price is almost everywhere independent of loss conditional on cost. Expert incentives depend on the margin and acceptance probability, not directly on client harm. The authors reduce the two-dimensional model to expected losses conditional on costs under their positive-correlation setup.
qs: The expert’s equilibrium price is only dependent on his cost, never on the consumer’s loss.
The consumer’s equilibrium inference therefore concerns the expected losses conditional on cost.

kp.k: Additional experts need not eliminate monopoly-like outcomes
kp.d: With N ≥ 2 identical experts, a small positive cost after the first consultation, and experts unable to observe search histories, the single-expert pooling and separating outcomes remain symmetric equilibria. Identical expected offers make further search unprofitable. This is an existence result, not a claim that competition always fails: the authors expressly leave open asymmetric equilibria involving search.
qs: In equilibrium, therefore, a consumer does not search, which reinforces an expert’s ability to maintain monopoly power.
Third, we have only claimed the existence of a symmetric equilibrium: all experts follow the same pooling or separating equilibrium strategy in the single-expert model.
Indeed, there might be asymmetric equilibria in which diﬀerent experts use diﬀerent pricing strategies and consumers search for diﬀerent prices.

kp.k: Alternative costs produce both overtreatment and undertreatment
kp.d: When repair is efficient only for intermediate losses, while costs remain increasing, the authors find that separation fails but pooling remains robust. The pooling outcome treats some low losses inefficiently while excluding some worthwhile higher-loss repairs; the authors identify it as the unique equilibrium satisfying their belief refinement in this extension.
qs: First, the separating equilibrium will fail to exist.
It follows that the pooling equilibrium involves service over-provision at low losses and under-provision at high losses.
Moreover, the pooling equilibrium is the unique equilibrium that satisﬁes the Nonnegative Proﬁt Principle.

kp.k: Price commitment does not resolve equilibrium selection
kp.d: Hybrid equilibria combine pooling and separating intervals. Unlike the conventional binary model, posting a price menu in the continuous-loss model may leave multiple continuation equilibria. The authors cannot rank profits across hybrid outcomes or identify the profit-maximising menu, limiting claims about optimal pricing commitments.
qs: Although we can characterize the property of the hybrid equilibria, we are unable to rank their proﬁts.
As a result, we cannot pin down the price menu which yields the expert the highest proﬁt.
Second, price commitment may not be useful for selecting the most proﬁtable equilibrium because there are generally multiple equilibria following a price menu.

kp.k: Risk, partial repair and renegotiation remain unresolved
kp.d: The authors identify risk aversion, partial repair, information arriving during treatment and resulting price renegotiation as open extensions. They also propose studying verifiable treatment costs without expert liability for outcomes. These are research questions and qualifications, not established findings or predictions.
qs: First, we have assumed risk neutrality.
The only veriﬁable event is the restoration of the baseline utility, so partial repair is ruled out.
Renegotiation about price may have to happen because the ultimate repair costs may change.
Our framework can be used to analyze the case when treatment cost is veriﬁable but the expert is not liable for treatment outcome.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Liu and Ma make theoretical claims about information and incentives in credence-good markets, not claims about AI. Their central finding is that limiting an expert's diagnostic information can improve efficiency and profit.
pts.d: Legal services appear as one example of credence goods, but the paper does not model AI or predict AI-driven legal-market change. In its own domain, the authors find that all equilibria under their baseline perfect-diagnosis model are inefficient. Pooling prices reveal only an interval of possible losses and leave some efficiently repairable problems untreated; separating prices reveal losses precisely but require consumers sometimes to reject worthwhile repairs. Depending on the loss distribution and cost function, pooling can generate greater profit and social surplus than separation. When experts can publicly choose a diagnostic information structure, an appropriately designed binary signal can implement first-best repair decisions and allow the expert to extract the entire expected surplus. In the multiple-expert extension, the single-expert pooling and separating outcomes remain possible equilibria: competition need not eliminate the modeled inefficiency.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence basis is mathematical modeling and equilibrium analysis, not empirical data or AI performance testing.
pts.d: Liu and Ma derive perfect-Bayesian equilibrium properties, closed-form pooling and separating strategies, a condition comparing their profits and welfare, and a constructive binary-information result. They provide mathematical proofs, illustrative numerical examples, and extensions involving random costs and losses, multiple experts, alternative cost functions, and noisy diagnostic signals. Examples involving mechanics and medical tests motivate the framework rather than validate its predictions. References to previous laboratory and field studies situate the paper in the literature; they are not new empirical tests of this model.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: These are static, conditional theoretical results with no adoption forecast or calendar timeframe.
pts.d: The baseline assumes risk-neutral consumers and experts, continuously distributed losses, increasing repair costs, nonverifiable costs and losses, and expert liability for eliminating the loss after an offer is accepted. Efficient repair in the main model is confined to losses below a threshold. The first-best information-design result requires the diagnostic test's selection and structure to be public information, while its signal remains private to the expert; the actual loss becomes known during repair only after the price is agreed. The authors explicitly caution that consumers may not understand such tests in practice. Noisy tests can produce both excessive and insufficient repairs, with outcomes converging to first best as noise disappears. The multiple-expert result assumes identical experts, positive search costs after the first visit, and experts who do not observe search histories; it establishes existence of symmetric equilibria rather than uniqueness.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The modeled effects concern expert providers and consumers of credence goods: information changes repair provision, provider profit, consumer surplus, and incentives to seek second opinions.
pts.d: Experts may earn more by revealing coarse rather than precise information, and optimally chosen coarse diagnostics can let them capture all expected gains from efficient trade. Consumers face insufficient repairs under the baseline equilibria. In the highlighted pooling equilibrium they have zero expected surplus but may gain or lose relative to their actual avoided loss; in separation they have zero surplus at each realized loss. First-best information design increases total surplus without giving consumers positive expected surplus. Some repairs then generate ex post losses for the expert, offset by profits on other repairs. In the symmetric multiple-expert equilibria, consumers do not seek further opinions because they expect identical offers and must pay search costs. The paper does not distinguish law-firm types, legal occupations, enterprise buyers, or AI providers, and does not demonstrate these effects specifically in legal services.
